title: The Bell of the Ninth Floor
premise: Folklorist Wendell Sterling arrives in the hollow of Ashenmoor to record a harvest song that locals will sing only once, never twice, and never in front of her camera. She discovers the song is a counting ritual: each verse names a household, and when the ninth verse is sung on harvest moon night, an extra chair appears in every home — and whatever sits in it takes one of the family before dawn. The village's founding families have kept the bell of the ninth floor ringing for two centuries to hold the count at bay, but the last ringer has died and the town council plans to let the debt fall on outsiders. Wendell must learn the true ninth verse, get the family she has come to love out ahead of the count, and choose between ringing the bell herself — binding her forever to Ashenmoor — or letting justice fall outside any law, on the descendants who built their prosperity on the ritual.
about_author: P. M. Villalobos is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing oral histories in rural mountain communities before turning to fiction. They write horror about records, rituals, and the terrible arithmetic of small towns.

chapters.title: The Song They Sing Once
chapters.summary: Wendell Sterling's POV. She arrives in Ashenmoor with recording equipment and a grant deadline, chasing a harvest song no archive holds twice. The innkeeper sings four verses for her, then goes pale and refuses a second take. Emotional beat: curiosity sharpening into unease as the whole room goes quiet around her recorder.

chapters.title: Grandma's House Has Nine Rooms
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Lodging with the Okafor family at the edge of the hollow, she photographs the farmhouse for her field notes. Every print shows a tenth chair at the table that isn't there. Grandma Adaeze burns the photos without explanation. Emotional beat: the first crack in Wendell's belief that documentation protects you.

chapters.title: The Bell You Can't Climb To
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. She maps the town and finds the old grange hall has nine floors by every count except the stairwell, which stops at eight. A boy named Tobias dares her to listen at midnight: the bell rings anyway. Emotional beat: wonder curdling into dread; the architecture itself is lying.

chapters.title: Verse Five Names a Family
chapters.summary: Alternating Wendell and Grandma Adaeze POVs. Adaeze finally explains: the song is a census, and the fifth verse once named the Okafors' predecessors, who vanished in a single night. The extra chair means your household has been counted. Emotional beat: grief and defiance — Adaeze refuses to be folklore.

chapters.title: The Council of Kept Ledgers
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. She attends a town meeting and meets Councilman Harrow Voss, whose family has rung the bell for six generations. He offers her funding, access, anything — if she leaves before the harvest moon. Emotional beat: charm with teeth; Wendell realizes she's being managed, not welcomed.

chapters.title: What the Photographs Remember
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Reviewing a century of archived village photographs, she finds the chair appearing in images decades apart — always in homes that later lost someone. Her own documentation has become evidence, and something has noticed her noticing. Emotional beat: the archivist's faith in records turns against her.

chapters.title: Tobias Sings the Sixth Verse
chapters.summary: Tobias Okafor's POV. The boy, curious and reckless, sings a fragment he overheard; that night his mother counts eleven chairs. Adaeze smashes two with an iron poker and they simply return. Emotional beat: guilt and terror — innocence has consequences here.

chapters.title: The Ringer's Room
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Voss gives her a tour of the grange's eighth floor: the Ringer's quarters, preserved like a shrine, its last occupant dead three weeks. His ledger shows the ritual's cost — one ringer per generation, taken by the bell. Emotional beat: Wendell understands what 'staying' really means in Ashenmoor.

chapters.title: Justice Outside the Law
chapters.summary: Adaeze's POV. Flashback chapter: forty years ago, Adaeze's husband tried to take the town's ritual debt to the county sheriff and courts. The paperwork vanished; the sheriff forgot him by morning; he was found seated in the extra chair. Emotional beat: bitter clarity — the law cannot hear this song.

chapters.title: The Count Begins Early
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. With the ringer dead and the moon waxing, chairs begin appearing across the hollow ahead of schedule. Three households are emptied in one night. Voss publicly blames Wendell's recordings for waking the count. Emotional beat: panic spreading; the village needs a scapegoat more than a solution.

chapters.title: The Verse Nobody Wrote Down
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Following the dead ringer's marginalia, she learns there is a ninth verse that unbinds a household from the count — but it was never transcribed because singing it requires naming what sits in the chair. Emotional beat: grim resolve; the answer exists and it is unbearable.

chapters.title: Loyalty Weighs More Than Truth
chapters.summary: Adaeze and Wendell's alternating POV. Adaeze begs Wendell to take the Okafors and go, abandoning the rest of the hollow. Wendell's recordings could expose everything, but exposure would scatter the villagers into a world that won't believe them. Emotional beat: the central loyalty-versus-truth collision, raw and unresolved.

chapters.title: Voss's Inheritance
chapters.summary: Harrow Voss's POV. We see his childhood: trained to ring, taught that the Voss name exists to feed the bell so everyone else stays fed. He offers Wendell a bargain — help him complete the count cleanly and he'll exempt the Okafors. Emotional beat: pity for a man shaped into an instrument.

chapters.title: The Empty Ninth Floor
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. She breaks into the grange at night and climbs past the eighth-floor landing into a stairwell that shouldn't exist, finding the bell room empty, cold, and waiting — with ten chairs arranged beneath the rope. Emotional beat: awe and violation; she has entered the story she was only documenting.

chapters.title: What Sits in the Chair
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. In the bell room she encounters the count itself — a presence wearing the accumulated faces of everyone the ritual ever took, including, briefly, her own. It speaks in the cadence of the song and offers her a place at the table instead of a place in it. Emotional beat: temptation framed as mercy.

chapters.title: The Recording That Sang Back
chapters.summary: Tobias's POV. Playing Wendell's field tapes, Tobias hears the missing verses sung by a voice that isn't hers. The tape completes itself overnight. Now anyone can trigger the count — including the council, who seize her equipment. Emotional beat: dread of knowledge weaponized; documentation cuts both ways.

chapters.title: Harvest Moon Eve
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. The town prepares: salt on thresholds, iron pokers, packed cars that won't start. Voss locks down the roads 'for safety.' Adaeze and Wendell finalize the escape plan — leave before moonrise, outrun the count. Emotional beat: taut, exhausted solidarity on the edge of ruin.

chapters.title: The Road Out Is Counted Too
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. The Okafors flee at dusk; the highway loops them back to the hollow no matter which direction they drive. The count doesn't stop at the town line — it stops where the song is known. Emotional beat: claustrophobic despair; there is no outside.

chapters.title: The Ninth Verse, Sung Twice
chapters.summary: Climax, Wendell's POV. On the ninth floor under the rising moon, Wendell does what no folklorist should: she sings the forbidden verse twice — once to name the thing in the chair, once to release it — breaking the cycle by giving the count a truth it was built to avoid. The bell rings without a hand. Emotional beat: sacrificial courage; the record becomes the ransom.

chapters.title: The Debt Reassigned
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. The broken ritual seeks its architects. The Voss ledger burns page by page, and Harrow chooses to sit in the final chair himself, ending his family's six-generation cruelty with an act of penance. Emotional beat: tragic justice outside any court; corruption paying its own interest.

chapters.title: After the Count
chapters.summary: Adaeze's POV. Dawn finds the hollow diminished but free; the grange now has only eight floors, and the chairs are gone from every photograph. The village begins deciding what to remember aloud. Emotional beat: cautious grief and tentative hope; survival is not the same as healing.

chapters.title: The Song They Sing Again
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV, epilogue. Months later, Wendell publishes nothing. Instead she returns to Ashenmoor each harvest, and the villagers teach her the song verse by verse — sung twice now, on purpose, as remembrance rather than summons. Her final recording ends with laughter in the background. Emotional beat: quiet redemption; some prayers are meant to be shared.
